chunks: Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Ibn Mahboub, from Abu Hafs Al-A'sha, from Amr [Umar] ibn Khalid, from Abu Hamza al-Thumali, from Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him), who said:

I went out until I reached this wall and leaned against it, and behold, there was a man wearing two white garments looking at my face. Then he said, 'O Ali ibn al-Husayn, why do I see you as gloomy and sad? Is it over the world? For the sustenance of Allah is present for the righteous and the immoral.' I said, 'I do not grieve over this, and it is as you say.'
He said, 'So is it over the Hereafter? For the promise of Allah is true, and a Dominant King [or he said: All-Powerful] will judge in it.' I said, 'I do not grieve over this, and it is as you say.'
He said, 'From what is your grief?' I said, 'From what we fear from the strife of Ibn al-Zubayr and what the people are enduring in it.'

He laughed, then said, 'O Ali ibn al-Husayn, have you seen anyone who supplicated to Allah but He did not answer him?' I said, 'No.' He said, 'Have you seen anyone who relied upon Allah but He did not suffice him?' I said, 'No.' He said, 'Have you seen anyone who asked Allah but He did not give him?' I said, 'No.' Then he disappeared from me.
ai.seo_question: What is the evidence for the reliability of Allah's response to supplication and reliance?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Imam Ali ibn al-Husayn (AS) is consoled by a figure, widely interpreted by Shia scholars as the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) or the Mahdi (AJ), during the political turmoil of Ibn al-Zubayr. The dialogue emphasizes the certainty of divine response to supplication and reliance (*tawakkul*), using a rhetorical triad to reassure the Imam that his anxiety over worldly strife is unfounded given Allah's consistent faithfulness to His servants.
